sentences: Ask the question at the table: where does this chicken come from?
What about these tomatoes?
What about this cheese?
Few people can answer precisely.
This is not a criticism.
Modern supply chains are long and intentionally discreet.
Labels help, but not as much as we think.
"Made in France" means that the processing took place in France, not necessarily that the ingredients come from there.
A French biscuit can contain wheat, sugar, and oil from three different continents.
For meat, the origin is better defined, but the label can distinguish the place of birth, raising, and slaughter — which are not always the same.
Should we then try to know everything?
That would be exhausting and a bit vain.
A few simple guidelines are often enough.
The first is the season.
A seasonal product has rarely traveled far or grown in a heated greenhouse.
It is generally cheaper, better, and more energy-efficient.
The second is the degree of processing.
The more ingredients a product has, the harder it becomes to trace its origin.
The third is the circuit.
Buying directly from a producer does not guarantee quality, but it at least allows you to ask the question — and get an answer.
There is finally a less practical interest.
Knowing that an apple takes months to ripen, that cheese requires aging, and that a chicken takes several weeks to grow changes the way we view its price.
What we call "expensive" sometimes seems less so when we know what it entails.

sentences: We like to think that our purchases are thoughtful: we compare, we evaluate, we decide.
Behavioral economics research tells a different story.
Let's take a common example.
In a store, an item is displayed as '€80 instead of €120.'
Our brain doesn't really remember the price: it remembers the difference.
We feel like we've saved forty euros, even though we've spent eighty.
The reference price serves as an anchor, and it is often chosen precisely for that reason.
Another well-known mechanism: the pain of payment.
Paying in cash physically makes you notice the expense.
Paying contactlessly, in one second, makes it almost invisible.
Several studies show that we spend more when the act of paying is less concrete.
Payments in installments amplify the effect even more: 'four times twenty-five euros' seems smaller than one hundred euros, even though it's the same amount.
Finally, there's artificial scarcity.
'Only two left in stock,' 'offer valid today': these messages trigger an ancient reaction, the fear of missing out.
They don't inform us; they pressure us.
Understanding this doesn't make anyone completely rational.
These mechanisms work even when we know about them.

But we can set up a few simple safeguards: wait twenty-four hours before any unplanned purchase, look at the final price rather than the discount, and ask ourselves not 'is this a good deal?' but 'would I have wanted it at the normal price?'
This last question, asked honestly, often reduces the desire.
It's not deprivation.
It's simply taking back the decision.

sentences: France is not known as a dry country.
It receives abundant rainfall and has significant underground water reserves.
However, for several summers now, water restrictions have been implemented in most departments.
How can we explain this discrepancy?
The problem is not so much the total amount as the distribution over time.
Rainfall has become more irregular: intense episodes in autumn and winter, followed by long dry spells in summer.
However, heavy rain runs off and flows back into rivers; it doesn't recharge the aquifers well.
It is the slow winter rains that fill the reserves.
In addition, there is a demand that increases precisely when the resource decreases: agricultural irrigation in summer, tourism in the already driest regions.
It is useful to know the distribution of uses.
In France, agriculture accounts for a majority of the water actually consumed throughout the year, especially in summer.
Domestic drinking water represents a much smaller share, even though it is the most visible.
This does not make domestic savings useless — they matter locally, and they serve as an example.
But we won't solve the issue with shorter showers.
The discussed solutions mainly concern infrastructure and usage.
Repairing the networks, where a significant portion of the water is lost through leaks.
Adapting crops to the available resources.
Reusing treated wastewater, which France still practices very little compared to other countries.
These choices are technical but also political.
Deciding who can use water, and for what purpose, will be one of the questions of the coming decades.

sentences: We have gotten used to reading the news for free.
This apparent free access has consequences that are useful to understand.
Producing information is expensive.
Sending a journalist out into the field, verifying documents, conducting an investigation over several months: all of this requires salaries and time, sometimes for just one article.
Historically, this cost was covered by two sources: newspaper sales and advertising.
Classified ads, in particular, have long financed a large part of local journalism.
The internet has caused these two pillars to collapse.
Ads have moved to specialized platforms, and online advertising brings in much less than print advertising, with most of the revenue being captured by a few very large companies.
The consequences are visible.
Many local newspapers have disappeared or merged.
However, local journalism is precisely what covers city councils, courts, and decisions that affect daily life.
Research shows that the disappearance of a local newspaper is accompanied by a decrease in voter participation and less oversight of public spending.
Several models are trying to compensate: digital subscriptions, crowdfunding, public support, foundations.
Each raises its own questions of independence, and none has yet replaced what has been lost.
There is a collective choice here, rarely expressed this way.
Quality information is not a good that appears spontaneously.
If no one pays for it, someone will eventually finance it for reasons other than informing us.

sentences: The phrase "It's cheaper" is probably the most powerful sales argument there is.
It seems undeniable: for the same product, why pay more?
However, the question deserves to be turned around.
A low price is not the same as a low cost.
When a product is inexpensive, the difference is almost always paid somewhere.
It can be paid through durability.
A cheap item that breaks after a year and needs to be replaced three times ends up costing more than a solid item bought once.
The displayed price lies about the real cost.
It can be paid by someone.
A very cheap garment implies very low manufacturing costs, and therefore very low wages, somewhere, for people we don't see.
It can be paid by the environment.
A price that does not account for the pollution produced or the resources depleted is an incomplete price.
Nature pays the difference, and often a future generation does too.
It can finally be paid collectively.
Certain activities that are very profitable for a company create costs borne by society — healthcare, pollution cleanup, social assistance.
Seeing these hidden costs does not mean that one always has to pay more.
Many people do not have a choice, and blaming the less fortunate would be unfair.
This is precisely why price cannot be the only regulator.
But for those who have some leeway, the useful question changes.
Not "how much does it cost?", but "who pays the difference?".
Once you see this question, you never see it quite the same way again.

sentences: The young people of today no longer respect anything. They are lazy, individualistic, and addicted to their screens. These phrases seem to describe our time.
However, we can find equivalents in texts that are several centuries old, sometimes from antiquity.
This continuity is striking, and it deserves reflection.
If each generation really degenerated, as these complaints suggest, humanity would have long been at the bottom of the abyss.
This is clearly not the case.
So why does this criticism repeat itself, almost identically?
Several mechanisms combine.
The first is a memory effect.
As we age, we remember our own youth selectively, forgetting its excesses.
We therefore compare an idealized youth to a real youth, which is inherently unfair.
The second is the misunderstanding of new practices.
Each generation grows up with tools that the previous one does not master.
These tools seem trivial or dangerous to those who have not integrated them.
It has been said about the novel, then about cinema, and then about television that they would dull the youth.
The third is deeper: the difficulty of accepting that the world changes and escapes us.
Criticizing the young is sometimes a refusal to age.
None of this means that no evolution is concerning.
Some truly are, and we need to be able to talk about them.
But we must distinguish them from automatic complaints.
The right reflex, in response to a 'things were better before,' is to ask ourselves: is this a real observed problem, or the refrain that each generation sings as they age?
Often, it's the refrain.
And one day, it will be the criticized young people who will sing it in turn.

sentences: After measuring the power of the devices that capture our attention, one question remains: what to do?
Simply "making an effort" is not enough, as we've seen, since the game is uneven.
Regaining control of our attention is not just a matter of willpower; it requires organization, method, and no illusions.
The first principle is to modify your environment rather than rely on your discipline.
Our willpower is a limited resource that quickly gets depleted; it's pointless to call on it at every moment.
It's better to act upstream: turn off notifications, remove the most captivating apps from your phone, and physically distance the screen during work or meals.
You can't resist a temptation you don't encounter.
The second principle is to rehabilitate boredom.
We've gotten into the habit of filling every little void — a queue, a journey, a break — by immediately grabbing our phone.
However, these empty moments have value: it's often in boredom that the mind wanders, reflects, and invents.
By systematically filling them, we deprive ourselves of precious time.
Accepting to be bored sometimes is to give the mind back a space that had been taken from it.
The third principle is to deliberately cultivate long attention.
Just as a flood of interruptions weakens it, regular practice strengthens it.

Reading an entire book, listening to a piece of music without doing anything else, walking without headphones: these seemingly modest practices retrain a faculty that the surrounding world tends to atrophy.
Finally, it's important to approach all of this without guilt.
The goal is not to give up digital tools, which provide immense services, nor to judge ourselves harshly for every slip.
It's about restoring a more equitable balance of power, where we decide our attention, not machines designed to capture it.
Our attention is what we have that is most precious: it is through it that we connect with the world, with others, and with ourselves.
Defending it is not a whim; it is to safeguard the very fabric of our inner life.

sentences: It has never been easier to meet someone.
Apps put thousands of potential partners at our fingertips, which we can sort, compare, and contact with a simple gesture.
In theory, this abundance should make love more accessible than ever.
In practice, many report the opposite: they have never had so many choices, nor found it so difficult to form attachments.
This paradox deserves our attention.
The first effect of unlimited choice is to change our perspective on others.
Faced with an apparently endless offer, each person we meet becomes just one option among others, compared to those that might follow.
Why invest in an imperfect relationship when a more attractive profile seems just a gesture away?
This logic, borrowed from consumerism, clashes with what love requires: patience, commitment, and acceptance of imperfections.
The second effect is more subtle.
By choosing too much, we end up not knowing how to choose.
Psychology has shown that, beyond a certain threshold, an abundance of options does not liberate: it paralyzes.
We hesitate, we procrastinate, we always keep a door open, for fear of giving up something better.
And by wanting to reserve the best for ourselves, we often miss out on the good.
This is not about condemning these tools, which have also allowed countless couples to form, and which help those whom life has not brought together.
The problem is not the tool, but the mindset it encourages: that of the consumer who compares, never quite satisfied, always in search of the ideal option that, by definition, does not exist.
Loving perhaps requires, at its core, the opposite of what unlimited choice promises.
Not finding the perfect person among an infinity of possibilities, but deciding to commit to a real person, with their flaws, and to build something with them rather than continuing to search.
Commitment is not the end of freedom; it may be its deepest use.
In a world that constantly invites us to keep all our options open, truly choosing someone — and giving up, for them, all the others — has become an act almost counter to the current trend.
Perhaps this is what gives it, today more than ever, its value.

sentences: The climate crisis reveals a deep weakness in our societies: their difficulty in thinking and acting for the long term.
The efforts we are being asked to make today will only bear fruit in decades, and will mainly benefit generations we will never know.
However, acting now for a distant future, at the cost of immediate sacrifices, goes against powerful trends, both individual and collective.
On an individual scale, our minds are such that they give much more weight to the present than to the future.
Immediate satisfaction attracts us more than a distant benefit, even if it is greater.
This trait, undoubtedly useful to our distant ancestors, whose survival depended on day-to-day existence, works against us in the face of threats whose effects unfold over generations.
We know the danger, but it seems abstract, distant, and easy to push off to later.
On a collective scale, the obstacles are no less significant.
Political leaders are elected for short terms and judged on immediate results.
Devoting resources to a problem whose benefits will only appear long after they have left holds little appeal for them.
The markets, for their part, value quick returns and care little for a horizon that extends beyond a few years.
Our institutions, as a whole, are built for the short term.
This shortsightedness is not a fatality; rather, it is a challenge to be met.
Other eras, other cultures, have been able to think beyond their own existence.
Those who planted trees whose shade they would never see, or built cathedrals they would not see completed, acted for a future that transcended them.
This capacity exists within us; it is a matter of reviving it.
Achieving this requires transforming our relationship with time.
This involves education, which can teach us to project ourselves beyond the immediate.
This involves rethought institutions, capable of representing the interests of future generations in present decisions.
This finally involves a narrative: that of a responsibility that connects us to those who will come after us, just as we are connected to those who preceded us.
Thinking long term is not natural; it is a conquest, a discipline, almost a virtue.
The climate crisis forces us to acquire it.
Perhaps this is, in the end, one of the few benefits it could bring us: forcing us to finally become the guardians of a future that transcends us.

sentences: Among all the body's needs, sleep is undoubtedly the one we treat with the most nonchalance.
We often boast about sleeping little, we cut back on our nights to work or have fun, and we see sleep as wasted time that it would almost be virtuous to reduce.
This attitude, however widespread it may be, is based on a profound misunderstanding of what sleep really is and what it accomplishes.
For sleeping is not doing nothing.
While we sleep, our body is far from inactive: it repairs itself, consolidates memory, regulates emotions, maintains immune defenses, and eliminates waste accumulated in the brain.
Sleep is not an interruption of life, but one of its essential processes, as vital as food.
Neglecting it is not saving time; it is sabotaging an essential task.
The consequences of chronic sleep deprivation are considerable, and research continues to clarify its extent.
Mentally, it impairs concentration, judgment, mood, and memory.
Physically, it is associated with an increased risk of many diseases.
A mind and body deprived of sleep function poorly, even when the person suffering from it, accustomed to their state, no longer realizes it.
For the lack of sleep is deceptive in that it makes us poor judges of our own abilities.
How then can we explain that we mistreat it to such an extent?
Partly because its effects are delayed and invisible: a night too short does not have immediate consequences, and one can be under the illusion for a long time about their ability to 'hold on.'
Partly also because our culture values activity and despises rest, as if sleeping were an admission of weakness or laziness.
We sacrifice our sleep on the altar of productivity, which paradoxically suffers as a result.
Rehabilitating sleep therefore requires a change in perspective.
It is not a favor we grant our body when we have the leisure, but a fundamental need that must be respected.
This involves concrete actions — regular schedules, a calm and dark room, a distance from screens in the evening — but above all a conviction: that the time spent sleeping is never wasted time.
Sleeping well is not a luxury or laziness; it is one of the most basic conditions for a healthy life.
By neglecting our sleep, we are neglecting ourselves.

sentences: A book is bought, a film is sold, a song is monetized.
Culture, clearly, is also an economy: it employs, it generates revenue, it is exchanged in substantial markets.
Should we conclude that a work is a product like any other, subject to the same laws as any merchandise?
The question is not merely theoretical: the answer we give affects how a society treats its artistic creation.
On one hand, it would be naive to deny the economic dimension of culture.
Artists need to make a living, works have production costs, and their distribution requires resources.
To claim that art is above any material consideration would reflect a comfortable idealism, often held by those who do not have to make a living from it.
A work indeed has economic value, and ignoring this does a disservice to both creators and the public.
But reducing culture to its only market dimension, treating it exactly like any product, poses a serious danger.
For if we judge a work solely by its commercial success, we end up producing only what sells best, to the detriment of what has value without necessarily reaching a wide audience.
The logic of the market favors what immediately pleases the greatest number, not what is demanding, new, or disturbing.
Left to its own devices, it would impoverish creation by eliminating everything that does not immediately find its market.
That is why most societies have believed that culture should not be left solely to the laws of commerce.
They have established protections, supports, exceptions: subsidies, regulated prices, creation aids, public institutions.
These measures are based on a conviction: culture is not a commodity like any other, because it fulfills a function that the market alone cannot ensure.
It transmits a heritage, nourishes debate, shapes minds, expresses what a society holds most profound.
This conviction is not without tensions or abuses, and we can discuss the forms that support for culture should take.
But the principle remains: a work is not just a commodity, because its value is not measured solely by what it brings in.
A book that hardly sells can be immensely valuable; a commercial success may have no lasting significance.
The market measures one thing; cultural value is another.
Treating culture as an ordinary commodity would thus mean forgetting what makes it precious.

Not that it should be removed from any economy — that is impossible and would not be desirable — but because it needs protection from a logic that, if left alone, would reduce it to what sells, sacrificing what is valuable.

sentences: Think for yourself: this is a piece of advice that everyone agrees with and believes they follow.
Nothing seems more desirable than the autonomy of thought, this ability to judge for oneself rather than to follow others blindly.
But as soon as you think about it, the phrase turns out to be more obscure than it appears.
What does it really mean to think for oneself?
And is it even possible?
This question, which concludes our exploration of belief and judgment, ties together its threads.
A first, naive conception of "thinking for oneself" means owing nothing to anyone, forming one's opinions alone, based solely on one's own mind, without relying on others.
But this conception is untenable.
No one thinks from nothing: we inherit a language, knowledge, and concepts, without which we couldn't even begin to think.
Almost everything we know comes from others, and claiming to verify everything by oneself would be absurd and impossible.
Anyone who would reject everything they haven't discovered alone wouldn't think any better; they would think almost nothing.
Thinking for oneself cannot therefore mean thinking without others.
It means rather thinking with others, but without surrendering one's judgment to them.
The difference is crucial.

It's not about rejecting everything that comes from others, but about not accepting it blindly; relying on the knowledge and opinions of others while retaining the ability to examine, weigh, and question them.
The autonomy of thought is not isolation, but a way of receiving: critical, active, never fully submissive.
This autonomy has its enemies.
The first is conformity, which leads us to adopt the opinions of those around us without examining them, simply out of a desire to belong, to not disturb.
The second is misunderstood authority, which makes us believe something because a prestigious figure asserts it, without asking whether their reasons are valid.
The third is laziness, which prefers ready-made opinions to the effort of judgment.
Thinking for oneself means resisting these three tendencies: daring to step away from the group, questioning authority, making the effort to judge rather than just receive.
But this autonomy also has its illusions, against which one must guard.
The first is confusing thinking for oneself with thinking against everyone, as if originality were in itself proof of clarity.
However, systematically rejecting what others think is another form of dependence, in the negative: one is still determined by them, always thinking the opposite.
The second illusion is believing that one thinks for oneself when one is merely following another herd, the one that believes it is precisely independent.
True autonomy is neither conformity nor systematic contradiction; it is judgment.

Thinking for oneself, in essence, is therefore not about producing one's opinions alone, nor opposing everyone, but exercising one's judgment on what one receives: welcoming the knowledge and ideas of others, but filtering them through reason; trusting those who know, but without giving up understanding; changing one's mind when necessary, without yielding to all pressures.
It is an ideal never fully achieved, a constant effort to be renewed.
But it is also what gives dignity to a free spirit: not knowing everything alone, but never abdicating one's capacity to judge.

sentences: As machines become more capable, performing tasks once thought to be exclusive to humans, imitating our creations and sometimes our behaviors, an age-old question arises with new urgency: what is uniquely human about us?
For a long time, we have defined ourselves by what only we could do — calculate, reason, create, speak.
But as machines catch up to us in these areas, these definitions begin to falter, and we are forced to look elsewhere for what distinguishes us.
This search, imposed by technology, may be one of the most fruitful of our time.
We must first rid ourselves of a defensive reflex that consists of seeking our specificity in certain abilities that machines have not yet matched.
This strategy is doomed to fail, as it constantly retreats: every time we define humanity by an ability, machines eventually imitate it, and we must fall back to another.
Defining ourselves by what machines cannot yet do condemns us to perpetual redefinition and endless anxiety.
Our humanity does not reside in performance, as every performance is, in principle, imitable.
Perhaps we should look not at what we do, but at what we are and experience.

What distinguishes humans may not be a superior ability, but a way of existing: having consciousness, feeling, suffering, enjoying, giving meaning, knowing that we will die, and living in light of that knowledge.
A machine can imitate the results of our activities, but does it feel anything?
Does it have an interiority, an experience, a relationship to its own existence?
Nothing indicates that.
What would be uniquely ours is not to do this or that, but to live it, to have the experience, to exist for ourselves and not just to function.
This line of thought shifts the question in a fruitful way.
It suggests that our humanity does not depend on our functional superiority, but on our condition as conscious and vulnerable beings, capable of feeling and giving meaning.

And this condition, far from being threatened by machines, is even highlighted: by accomplishing without consciousness what we achieve by living, machines reveal to us that our value was not in the accomplishment, but in the lived experience that accompanied it.

It is not because we calculate that we are human, but because, in calculating, we experience something; the machine calculates without experiencing anything, and it is this difference, not the performance, that matters.
This reflection has practical implications, as it indicates what we should preserve and cultivate in a world of machines.

Not to compete with them in the realm of performance, where we will always be surpassed, but to deepen what is uniquely ours: the life of consciousness, the depth of experience, the capacity for meaning, and true relationships between beings who feel.

In a world where machines are increasingly doing what is functional, what will remain precious will be precisely what is not: presence, attention, shared experience, everything that pertains not to the accomplishment of a task, but to the meeting of consciousnesses.
Remaining human among machines is therefore not about clinging to a threatened superiority, nor imitating machines to avoid being left behind.
It is about cultivating what constitutes us: our condition as conscious, sensitive, mortal beings, capable of meaning and relationship.

Machines, by depriving us of our performances, may be doing us an unexpected service: forcing us to rediscover what, within us, was not reducible to a performance, and to finally cultivate it for its own sake.

The challenge is not to remain superior to machines, but to remain fully human — and this is not played out in the realm where machines catch up to us, but in the deeper realm where they do not follow us: that of lived life and felt meaning.

sentences: Who am I? The question seems so simple that we think it has already been resolved: I am me, a person identical to herself, who persists through time.
However, as soon as we reflect on it, this obviousness slips away.
For what makes me 'me', the same today as I was yesterday and will be in twenty years, while my body renews itself, my thoughts change, and I am no longer the child I once was?
On what does this identity that I so spontaneously attribute to myself rest?
This question, upon examination, turns out to be one of the deepest and most bewildering there is.
Let’s first seek what could ground personal identity.
Could it be the body?
But the body changes continuously; its cells renew themselves, it ages, transforms, to the point that the body of a child and that of an old person have almost nothing materially in common.
If I am my body, then I am not the same as I was thirty years ago, which contradicts the intuition of continuity.
The body, in perpetual renewal, provides a fragile foundation for an identity that is supposed to persist.
Could it then be consciousness, memory, this thread of memories that connects the moments of my life?
This answer is more appealing: I am the same because I remember having been, because a continuity of consciousness links my present to my past.
But it has its flaws.
My memory is patchy, selective, sometimes misleading; I have forgotten almost all of my existence, and entire parts of my past are as foreign to me as those of another.
If I am my memories, what happens to my identity for everything I have forgotten, or if I were to lose my memory?
Consciousness, too, provides an uncertain foundation.
Perhaps the mistake is to seek a fixed thing, a permanent core, a substantial 'me' that would remain identical amid change.

Some schools of thought suggest that no such core exists, that the 'me' is not a thing, but a process, a continuously changing flow of perceptions, thoughts, sensations, without a permanent substrate.
The 'me' would not be what remains identical amid change, but the name we give to this flow itself, to this dynamic continuity that has nothing fixed.
This conception, bewildering, dissolves identity by making it coincide with change itself.
Should we conclude that the 'me' is an illusion, that I am nobody, that there is no stable subject?
That would be drawing an excessive conclusion from a real difficulty.
For even if the 'me' is not a fixed thing, there is indeed a continuity, a unique perspective on the world, a story that is mine and not that of another.
This continuity may not be that of an immutable substance, but that of a narrative, a project, a perspective that maintains itself through change by integrating it.
I am not a fixed thing; I am a story that continues, an identity that is built rather than found.
This conception has liberating consequences.
If the 'me' is not a fixed core to be discovered, but a story that is built, then I am not condemned to be what I have been; I can change, become something else, rewrite my narrative.
Identity is not a given to which one must be faithful, but a work to which I am committed.
'Who am I?' therefore does not call for the discovery of a hidden essence, but for the continued invention of oneself.
We are not things that have an identity; we are beings that are made, and this absence of a fixed core, far from being a loss, is the condition of our freedom to become.

sentences: Our societies consider themselves secularized: religion has retreated, the sacred seems to have given way to reason, the profane, and the disenchantment of the world.
It is often imagined that the sacred was specific to religious societies, and that by secularizing, our societies would have abolished it.
But this view may be misleading.

For the sacred — that which is set apart, regarded as intangible, surrounded by respect and prohibitions — has it really disappeared, or has it merely shifted, investing in other objects than those of religion?
Questioning the persistence of the sacred in a world that believes itself disenchanted is revealing.
Let us recall what the sacred is, independent of any particular religion.
The sacred refers to that which is removed from ordinary use, regarded as intangible, surrounded by absolute respect, that which cannot be treated like other things nor transgressed without horror.
What is sacred escapes calculation, bargaining, and relativization; it imposes itself as an absolute, before which one must bow.

This structure — the setting apart of an intangible absolute — has long been upheld by religion, but it may not be essentially religious: it could invest in other objects, as long as a society holds something to be absolutely respectable.
However, our secularized societies do have their sacreds, even if they do not name them as such.

The dignity of the human person, for example, functions as a sacred: we regard it as intangible, absolute, removed from all calculation; transgressing the dignity of a human being horrifies us like a desecration.
Fundamental rights, the value of life, certain memories, certain places, are surrounded by a respect that has all the characteristics of the sacred.
We have desacralized traditional religious objects, but we have sacralized other things, which we hold to be absolute and intangible.
The sacred has not disappeared; it has changed its object.
This persistence of the sacred is not a residual archaism, but perhaps a necessity.
For a society needs to hold certain things as intangible, removed from calculation and relativization, lest it have nothing absolute to ground it.

If everything were relative, negotiable, calculable, if there were nothing that we hold as sacred in the sense of absolutely respectable, then nothing would resist utility, power dynamics, or bargaining.
The sacred, even when secularized, fulfills this function: it sets absolute limits, prohibitions that no calculation can lift, values before which even the majority must bow.
A completely desacralized society, where nothing would be held as absolute, would be a society without foundation, surrendered to mere power dynamics.
Recognizing the secular sacred has important implications.

It first invites us to understand that secularization is not the abolition of the sacred, but its displacement, and that our societies, which believe themselves disenchanted, have their own absolutes, their own intangibles, their own sacred prohibitions.
It also invites us to question these sacreds: what are they, are they just, what do they reveal about our values?
A society is largely defined by what it holds sacred, by what it refuses to treat as an ordinary thing; examining our sacreds is examining who we are.

It is not about regretting the religious sacred or advocating a return of religion, but about lucidly recognizing that the need for the sacred persists, that it still structures our societies in secularized forms, and that it fulfills a function we cannot do without without peril.
The disenchantment of the world has not abolished the sacred; it has transformed it, displaced it, secularized it.

Understanding this is to better understand ourselves, recognizing that even the most secularized society continues to hold certain things as absolute and intangible — and that perhaps it is there, in these secular sacreds, that its deepest and most worthy values reside.

sentences: The school presents itself as the ultimate instrument of equal opportunity: by offering the same education to everyone, it should enable each person, regardless of their background, to succeed based on their merit and thus correct the inequalities of birth.
This promise is at the heart of the legitimacy of modern schooling.
However, a critique developed by social sciences disturbingly questions this: far from correcting inequalities, the school might actually reproduce them, or even legitimize them.
This thesis, if valid, profoundly shakes the idea we have of school.
The argument for reproduction is based on an observation: academic results are strongly correlated with social background.
Children from privileged backgrounds succeed, on average, much better than those from working-class backgrounds.

If the school corrected the inequalities of birth, we should observe the opposite, or at least a mitigation; however, we see reproduction, with the school tending to confirm starting positions rather than overturning them.
This robust and repeated observation contradicts the promise of equal opportunity: the school, which is supposed to be a social elevator, largely functions as a mechanism for reproducing positions.
How can we explain this paradox?
Not through an overt inequality — the school does indeed offer the same education to all — but through more subtle mechanisms.

The school values a certain relationship to language, culture, and knowledge, which is not evenly distributed: children from privileged backgrounds arrive at school already familiar with the culture it values, possessing the codes, language, and references it expects, while children from working-class backgrounds must acquire everything.

By treating unequally prepared children identically, and valuing a culture that some already possess and others discover, the school, under the guise of formal equality, advantages those who started off ahead.
The equal treatment of unequal children perpetuates inequality.
There is something even more troubling in this critique.
The school does not merely reproduce inequalities; it legitimizes them by presenting them as the result of merit.

Since everyone has received the same education, the success of some and the failure of others seem to reflect their respective merits; the one who fails appears responsible for their failure, while the one who succeeds is deemed deserving of their success.
In this way, the school transforms social inequalities into seemingly deserved inequalities, masking the reproduction of starting positions under the veil of academic merit.
This may be its most insidious function: not only to reproduce inequalities but to legitimize them by presenting them as just.
Should we, in light of this critique, despair of the school, renouncing it as a sham?
That would be drawing an excessive and demobilizing conclusion.

For while the school largely reproduces inequalities, it is not merely a mechanism of reproduction; it also allows, to some extent, for mobility, emancipation, and the success of children whom nothing destined for that.
Recognizing the tendency to reproduce does not mean denying any emancipatory capacity; it means that this capacity is much less than claimed, and that it faces powerful mechanisms.
The critique does not invite us to abandon the school, but to stop naively believing that it spontaneously corrects inequalities, in order to act on what prevents it from doing so.
For recognizing that the school reproduces inequalities gives us the means to combat this reproduction.

If the equal treatment of unequal children perpetuates inequality, then correcting it requires treating differently those who are differently prepared, giving more to those who have received less, and compensating for initial inequalities rather than ignoring them under a formal equality.
This requires a school that does not merely offer the same to all, but is committed to reducing initial gaps, to transmitting to those who do not possess them the codes and culture it values.
The school can reproduce inequalities; it can also, if it becomes aware of them and takes the necessary steps, combat them.
But it will not do so spontaneously, by its mere existence: it requires a clear-sighted will, which begins by recognizing what the naive promise of equal opportunity has masked.

sentences: A tension runs through our relationship with belonging, which globalization has made more acute: should we aspire to be citizens of the world, belonging to all of humanity beyond borders, or recognize the need for rootedness, for a particular belonging to a place, a culture, a community?
On one hand, the cosmopolitan ideal of universal belonging, which transcends particularisms; on the other, the need for rootedness, for a concrete belonging without which one feels lost.

These two aspirations, equally legitimate, seem to oppose each other; and their reconciliation is one of the challenges of our time, where globalization and the need for roots compete for people's minds.
The ideal of the citizen of the world has its grandeur.

To want to be a member of all humanity, to feel concerned about the fate of all people, to refuse that borders limit our solidarity, is a noble aspiration that expands the heart beyond the narrowness of particular belongings.

Cosmopolitanism rejects self-absorption, national egoism, and indifference to what happens beyond its borders; it affirms a human community that transcends particularisms, a solidarity that does not stop at the limits of one's nation.
This universalist aspiration, when it is true to itself, is generous, open, and worthy.
But the cosmopolitan ideal also has its limits and illusions.
For a person does not belong to humanity in general in a concrete way; they first belong to a place, a culture, a particular community that shapes them, nourishes them, and gives them an identity.

To want to be a citizen of the world without a particular belonging risks an abstract belonging, without substance, without roots; it risks belonging to nothing concrete under the pretext of belonging to everything.
A person without roots, who feels from nowhere because they want to be from everywhere, is often a lost person, deprived of what gives identity, ground, and a world.
The need for rootedness is not an archaic notion to be overcome; it is a fundamental human need, without which one feels uprooted, lost, and without identity.
The need for rootedness thus has its legitimacy, which cosmopolitanism sometimes overlooks.

Belonging to a place, a culture, a community, having roots, a soil, a world that is one's own, is not a limitation to be transcended; it is a condition of human existence, providing identity, grounding, and a concrete world.
Humans need to belong to something particular, to feel like they are from somewhere, to have roots that nourish them.
To despise this need in the name of cosmopolitanism is to misunderstand human nature; it advocates for a rootlessness that impoverishes more than it liberates.
But the need for rootedness also has its dangers, which cosmopolitanism highlights.

For attachment to one's particular belonging can degenerate into withdrawal, exclusion, and hostility towards what is different; rootedness can become confinement, love for one's world can turn into disdain for others, and attachment to one's roots can lead to rejection of the foreigner.
History shows the excesses to which the exaltation of particular belonging can lead when it closes off, hardens, and stands against others.
The need for rootedness, legitimate as it is, can thus become perverted into narrow nationalism, xenophobia, and a rejection of the universal.
Wisdom may lie in reconciling these two aspirations, rather than choosing one over the other.
One can be rooted and open, belong to a particular place and feel like a member of humanity, love one's own world without despising others.
Rootedness and openness are not necessarily mutually exclusive; one can have roots and wings, belong concretely to a particular world while feeling connected to all of humanity.
True rootedness is not withdrawal, but the anchoring from which one can open up; true cosmopolitanism is not uprooting, but opening up from a place of rootedness.
Those who are well-rooted in their world can open up to others without losing themselves; those who are open to the world can remain true to their roots without becoming confined.

Being rooted and a citizen of the world, belonging to a particular place and to all of humanity, is perhaps the balance to seek — one that connects what we have said about the universal and the particular, about France and the world, about the foreigner and oneself: not one against the other, but one through the other, opening up from rootedness, the universal through the particular.

sentences: I must admit that it's quite a great misfortune, said the sergeant, that we came to settle on this peninsula just as it was about to break away from the continent and sail the seas!

Consider the time it took for these seeds of firs, birches, and strawberry trees to multiply, to become shrubs and trees!

sentences: In his name, adultery is stigmatized and condemned, not because it is a recklessness that leads to disillusionment and regret, but because it is a crime against the family.

You stigmatize and condemn suicide, not because it is madness — the madman is not responsible — nor because it is cowardice, as it sometimes requires a certain physical courage, but because it shows contempt for duty in a life that is ending, and is a cry of disbelief in a life that is beginning.

This morality stigmatizes realistic literature, not because it depicts passions — hatred, vengeance, love; the world revolves around these, and art must portray them — but when it depicts them without restraint or measure.
Art without rules is no longer art; it is like a woman who would shed all her clothing.
Imposing the sole rule of public decency on art does not enslave it, but honors it.
One only grows with a rule.
Here, gentlemen, are the principles we profess; here is a doctrine we defend with conviction.

Gustave Flaubert is accused before you of having written a bad book, of having, in this book, outraged public morality and religion.
